title: U.S. Immigration Courts Ordered Deportation in 87% of June Cases, Data Shows
excerpt: Federal immigration courts issued nearly 87,000 deportation orders in June 2026, the highest monthly rate on record, as Florida courts lead the nation in pending caseloads.
body:
• Immigration judges ordered deportation in 87.1% of completed cases in June 2026, issuing 78,882 removal orders and 7,689 voluntary departure orders out of 99,441 cases closed.
  • Florida's Miami-Dade County leads the country with 137,373 pending immigration court cases, the highest of any county in the United States.
  • Only 21.5% of immigrants facing removal orders had legal representation in June, as federal funding for legal aid programs faces cuts.

Record-High Deportation Rate

U.S. immigration courts ordered deportation in 87.1% of all cases completed in June 2026, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC) at Syracuse University. Judges issued 78,882 removal orders and granted voluntary departure to 7,689 immigrants out of 99,441 total cases completed that month.

https://x.com/Drill_BabyDR1LL/status/2080336115400077723

For fiscal year 2026 through June, immigration judges have issued deportation orders in 81.9% of completed cases, totaling 555,737 orders. Courts closed 687,353 cases while receiving 413,945 new ones, chipping away at a backlog that still stands at 3.195 million active cases.

The rate has climbed steeply under the Trump administration. In fiscal year 2023, removal orders accounted for 47% of case outcomes, according to Congressional Research Service data. That jumped to 50.5% in fiscal year 2025 before surging past 80% this year.

Florida at the Center

Florida sits at the epicenter of the nation's immigration court activity. Miami-Dade County has the largest pending caseload in the country at 137,373 cases, followed by Cook County, Illinois (108,934) and Queens County, New York (103,562). The Miami Immigration Court issued the most decisions of any court nationally in fiscal year 2024, with 46,933 cases completed.

Pressure on Florida's immigrant communities has intensified on multiple fronts. The Supreme Court's June ruling in Mullin v. Doe cleared the way for the administration to end Temporary Protected Status designations, putting more than 158,000 Haitians in Florida at risk of deportation, according to the Haitian Bridge Alliance.

Courts Accelerate With New Tactics

The surge coincides with aggressive new court procedures. According to NPR, courts have begun scheduling "mega master" calendar hearings with 100 or more respondents at a time, up from the typical two to three dozen. These hearings primarily target immigrants without lawyers.

"It's almost like they are being designed to increase how many people get deportation orders automatically."

— Vanessa Dojaquez-Torres, Practicing Policy Counsel, American Immigration Lawyers Association

The Justice Department has hired 153 new immigration judges this fiscal year, the most ever. But that followed the firing of more than 100 judges last year. An NPR analysis found judges with backgrounds representing immigrant clients were disproportionately let go.

Representation Gap Widens

Only 21.5% of immigrants had legal representation when they received removal orders in June 2026. Federal contracts providing lawyers to unaccompanied minors are under threat: the administration has not paid $65 million owed for legal services provided to 20,000 children, and the primary contract expires at the end of July.

"Removing legal representation does not make the immigration system more efficient, more effective or more just. It makes it less accurate, less reliable and less worthy of public confidence."

— Elizabeth Young, Former Immigration Judge

Only 1.76% of new cases filed in FY 2026 involved allegations of criminal activity beyond possible illegal entry, according to TRAC. The vast majority of respondents in immigration courts have no criminal record.

What Comes Next

A federal appeals court in June allowed the administration to expand expedited removal — deportation without a court hearing — to undocumented immigrants anywhere in the country. The administration is also activating the long-dormant Alien Terrorist Removal Court for the first time since its 1996 creation.

The top nationalities ordered deported in FY 2026 are Mexico (121,001), Honduras (67,257), Guatemala (65,359), Venezuela (65,105) and Colombia (36,651). Of the 3.195 million pending cases, 2.31 million involve immigrants who have filed formal asylum applications.
